passages.title: From Kitchen Scraps to Compost
passages.text:
From Kitchen Scraps to Compost

Plants need healthy soil, water, air and sunlight to grow. Gardeners can improve some soils by adding compost. Compost is made when tiny living things break down suitable plant and food scraps over time. It is not made by simply piling every kind of rubbish together.

At Willow Park School, the class wanted to use less of the fruit and vegetable waste from snack time. With their teacher's help, they set up a compost bin in a suitable outdoor spot. They added items such as fruit peels, vegetable leaves and dry fallen leaves. They left out plastic wrappers, glass and other rubbish because these materials do not break down in the same way.

The class learned that a compost pile needs a balance of materials. Fresh green scraps often contain more moisture, while dry leaves help add air spaces and absorb some extra moisture. The pile should be damp, like a squeezed sponge, rather than dripping wet or completely dry. An adult helped the children turn the pile carefully so air could reach the material.

Composting takes time. The children checked the bin each week and recorded what they noticed. At first, the scraps were easy to recognise. Later, many pieces became darker and harder to identify. The pile sometimes felt warm inside because tiny living things were active as they broke down the material. The class did not add new compost to the garden straight away; an adult checked that it was ready first.

When the compost was ready, the gardener mixed some into a flower bed. The children saw that compost was one way to return useful material to the soil instead of sending all suitable scraps to the rubbish bin. They also learned that compost alone could not replace the water, light and other conditions plants need.

The class made a simple guide showing what could and could not go into their bin. They shared it with other pupils and reminded everyone to ask an adult if they were unsure about an item. Their project showed that small, careful habits can reduce some waste and help a school garden, but the bin still needs the right materials, air, moisture and time.
